target.title: Decoding spoken words using local field potentials recorded from the cortical surface
target.version: Author manuscript; final edited form published 2010 Sep 1; issue date 2010 Oct

read.pdf: Fig. 1–6 and Supplementary Figs. 1–3 captions; Table 1 fully read in supplied text extraction

entries.text: The evaluation is a single-subject case study: one male patient with medically refractory epilepsy.
entries.condition: The participant required extraoperative ECoG monitoring; all reported decoding uses this one patient.
entries.quote: One male patient who required extraoperative ECoG monitoring for medically refractory epilepsy gave informed consent to participate in an institutional review board-approved study.

entries.text: Two subdural micro-electrode arrays each had 16 channels of 40-μm wire in a 4×4 grid with 1-mm spacing.
entries.unit: arrays, channels, wire diameter, grid, spacing
entries.condition: Arrays were nonpenetrating and placed beneath the dura over face motor cortex and Wernicke’s area.
entries.quote: A single 16-electrode 4×4 micro-ECoG grid shown next to a U.S. quarter-dollar coin.

entries.text: The task decoded repeatedly articulated spoken words, prompted verbally and cued visually.
entries.condition: Patient was instructed to repeat each word at approximately one-second intervals; this is overt vocalization, not imagined speech.

entries.text: The closed vocabulary contained ten words: yes, no, hot, cold, hungry, thirsty, hello, goodbye, more, and less.
entries.condition: Evaluation used combinations of two through ten of these prompted word classes.

entries.text: Sessions lasted approximately one hour on four consecutive days.
entries.condition: Single patient; the paper does not identify which session/day supplied each train/decode subset or report cross-day testing.

entries.text: For each word, 30 adjacent stereotyped trials were selected, with 15 for training and 15 for decoding.
entries.condition: Manually selected stereotyped articulations from the single patient; trials were adjacent, not described as an independent session or participant test set.
entries.quote: For each word, a subset of 30 adjacent trials (15 for training and 15 for decode) containing stereotypical articulation was selected for further analysis.

entries.text: Stereotypy was judged using inflection, pitch, and duration; more than half the trials were discarded for some words, including yes and hot.
entries.condition: Selection occurred before the described classifier analysis; the paper does not report a blinded or reproducible scoring procedure.
entries.quote: For some words, e.g. “yes” and “hot”, the pronunciation of words varied enough that more than half of the trials were discarded.

entries.text: Yes had 166 recorded trials, of which 81 were stereotyped.
entries.condition: Single patient across the experimental sessions; Table 1 counts precede the per-word selection of 30 adjacent trials for classification.

entries.condition: Single patient across the experimental sessions; Table 1 counts precede the per-word selection of 30 adjacent trials for classification.

entries.text: Neural signals were digitized at 30,000 samples/s after 0.3–7500-Hz bandpass filtering.
entries.condition: Recorded neural signals through 32 channels from the two arrays, referenced to the clinical reference lead.

entries.text: Chronux spectrograms used 400-ms windows, 100-ms steps, time-bandwidth product 5, and 9 leading tapers.
entries.unit: ms window; ms step; time-bandwidth product; tapers
entries.condition: Spectrograms generated from neural session time series; the paper identifies Chronux but not a specific software version or script.

entries.text: Spectrogram smoothing averaged four 0.9-Hz bands and six 100-ms time steps.
entries.unit: frequency bands × Hz; time steps × ms
entries.condition: Chronux spectrogram processing for the reported signal inspection.

entries.text: Each articulation was represented by 250 power features in 2-Hz bands from 0.3 to 500 Hz.
entries.condition: Features from each word used a 0.5-s articulation-aligned Hann-windowed segment per micro-electrode.

entries.text: Channels were re-referenced to the common average within each array; spectra were log-normalized across trials per electrode.
entries.condition: The paper gives the normalization description but not its formula or whether normalization statistics were fit on training trials only.

entries.text: PCA was fitted to the training matrix with 15 training articulations per word; each class centroid was the mean projected feature vector.
entries.condition: Closed-set classifier; PCA features could be selected from channel/trial subsets, and the fitted PCA/centroids were used for decoding.

entries.text: Decode trials were assigned to the nearest word centroid in PCA space.
entries.condition: Nearest-centroid classification of 15 additional trials per word; no language model or external lexical aid is described.

entries.text: Chance was defined as uniform random assignment among the included classes; for two classes the baseline was 0.5.
entries.condition: Authors applied the uniform class-assignment chance level to all evaluations.

entries.text: FMC features yielded 85.0 ± 13.1% mean accuracy (median 83.3%) over all 45 two-word combinations.
entries.condition: One male patient; 45 pairs from the ten-word vocabulary; features from all 16 FMC electrodes; 15 train and 15 decode trials per word selected from 30 adjacent stereotyped trials; no independent-session or subject test reported.

entries.text: Wernicke’s-area features yielded 76.2 ± 15.0% mean accuracy (median 76.7%) over the same 45 two-word combinations.
entries.condition: One male patient; features from all 16 Wernicke’s-area electrodes; same ten-word set, 45 pairs, adjacent 15/15 train/decode stereotyped-trial protocol; no independent-session or subject test reported.

entries.text: Joint FMC+Wernicke classification changed accuracy by only 0.40 ± 0.43 percentage points over FMC alone across two- through ten-word combinations.
entries.condition: One patient; 32 electrodes jointly versus 16 FMC electrodes alone; combinations of two to ten words; 15/15 train/decode adjacent stereotyped trials per word.
entries.quote: Joint classification did not improve performance over the level achieved by FMC electrodes alone (0.40 ± 0.43 percentage-point difference in the accuracy of two- through ten-word combinations).

entries.text: Selecting the best five FMC electrodes increased accuracy by 4.0 percentage points for two-word combinations, to 89.6 ± 10.8% (median 90.0%).
entries.condition: One patient; best five FMC electrodes; two-word combinations; 15/15 train/decode adjacent stereotyped trials per word; independence of electrode selection from evaluation data is not reported.
entries.quote: ranged from 4.0 percentage points (89.6 ± 10.8% accuracy, median 90.0, for two-word combinations)

entries.text: For ten-word classification, the best five FMC electrodes improved accuracy by 20.0 percentage points, with 48% accuracy.
entries.condition: One patient; ten-class closed-set decode; best five FMC electrodes; 15/15 train/decode adjacent stereotyped trials per word; selection/evaluation independence is not reported.
entries.quote: up to 20.0 percentage points (48% for the ten-word combination)

entries.text: The average best-five-versus-all-16 FMC improvement across word combinations was 13.5 ± 5.2 percentage points.
entries.condition: One patient; two- through ten-word combinations; best five FMC electrodes compared with all 16; adjacent 15/15 train/decode trials per word; electrode-selection independence not reported.
entries.quote: with 13.5 ± 5.2 percentage points difference on average

entries.text: Using the five best FMC electrodes together exceeded the same electrodes used independently by 16.1 ± 2.3 percentage points on average.
entries.condition: One patient; best five FMC electrodes, combined versus tested independently; word combinations and trial splits as in the paper’s classifier evaluation; channel-selection independence not reported.

entries.text: Selecting the five best Wernicke’s-area electrodes raised accuracy by 1.3 ± 0.7 percentage points on average.
entries.condition: One patient; best five Wernicke’s-area electrodes versus all 16, averaged across word combinations; train/decode split as above; electrode-selection independence not reported.
entries.quote: In contrast, selecting the five highest-performing electrodes over Wernicke’s area did not substantially improve performance (1.3 ± 0.7 percentage-point increase on average).

entries.text: The five best Wernicke’s-area electrodes together exceeded independent use of those electrodes by 5.0 ± 0.3 percentage points.
entries.condition: One patient; best five Wernicke’s-area electrodes, combined versus independent; word combinations and adjacent 15/15 trial splits as in the evaluation; channel-selection independence not reported.

entries.text: In two-word classification, accuracy rose above chance at 20 Hz, peaked at 110 Hz, and remained above chance through 500 Hz.
entries.condition: Single-feature frequency analysis of the two-word case using the classifier; one patient and trial protocol as above.

entries.text: For best-five-channel two-word decoding, median accuracy was 74.0%, 81.2%, 89.6%, and 88.1% with 0.1-, 0.25-, 0.5-, and 0.75-s windows, respectively.
entries.condition: One patient; two-word classifications; best five channels; windows of 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, and 0.75 s; adjacent 15/15 train/decode trials per word.

entries.text: FMC best-five-electrode pair accuracy ranged from 53% to 100%; 40 of 45 pairs reached at least 80%.
entries.condition: One patient; best five FMC electrodes; all 45 two-word pairs of the ten-word vocabulary; 15/15 adjacent stereotyped train/decode trials per word.

entries.text: Forty of 45 FMC word pairs were classified at 80% accuracy or better.
entries.condition: One patient; FMC best five electrodes; all pairs from the ten-word vocabulary; 15/15 adjacent stereotyped train/decode trials per word.

entries.text: Wernicke’s-area best-five-electrode pair accuracy ranged from 36.7% to 100%; 15 of 45 pairs reached at least 80%.
entries.condition: One patient; best five Wernicke’s-area electrodes; all 45 two-word pairs from the ten-word vocabulary; 15/15 adjacent stereotyped train/decode trials per word.

entries.text: Fifteen of 45 Wernicke’s-area word pairs were classified at 80% accuracy or better.
entries.condition: One patient; Wernicke’s-area best five electrodes; all pairs from the ten-word vocabulary; 15/15 adjacent stereotyped train/decode trials per word.

entries.text: An FMC electrode averaged 89.3% for the word no, while a neighbor 1 mm away averaged 87.8% for less.
entries.unit: % average accuracy; mm separation; % average accuracy
entries.condition: Each electrode’s word score averaged its two-word classifications involving that word; one patient; FMC array.

entries.text: A neighboring FMC electrode 1 mm away averaged 87.8% for less.
entries.condition: Per-electrode average across two-word classifications involving less; one patient; FMC array.

entries.text: Fifteen of 16 FMC electrodes had a neighbor within 1.4 mm whose best word differed, with that word classified at ≥75%.
entries.condition: Neighbors include diagonal grid positions; one patient; per-electrode word accuracies averaged over pairwise classifications.

entries.text: Fourteen of 16 Wernicke’s-area electrodes met the corresponding different-best-word neighbor criterion.
entries.condition: Neighbor within 1.4 mm, including diagonals; the neighboring electrode’s best word had at least 75% accuracy; one patient.

entries.text: For hot, neighboring FMC electrodes 1 mm apart averaged 84.4% versus 56.7% for the same word.
entries.condition: Per-electrode average across two-word classifications involving hot; one patient; FMC array.
entries.quote: one electrode over FMC classified the word “hot” with 84.4% average accuracy while a neighbouring electrode 1 mm away classified the same word with only 56.7% average accuracy

entries.text: Eight of 16 FMC and five of 16 Wernicke’s-area electrodes had a ≥15-percentage-point same-word difference from a neighbor.
entries.condition: Neighboring-electrode comparison for the same word; one patient; arrays at both sites.

entries.text: The authors report nearly 30% variation in same-word classification accuracy between individual electrodes 1 mm apart.
entries.condition: Single patient; individual micro-electrodes; same word; discussion-level summary of the observed topography.
entries.quote: Using micro-electrodes approximated to the scale of cortical processing, we found variation of nearly 30% in the classification accuracies (for the same word) of individual electrodes spaced 1 mm apart.

entries.text: Within 9 mm² over FMC, almost every electrode had a neighbor within 1.4 mm whose best-classified word differed.
entries.condition: One patient; FMC grid; statement is a discussion summary of the electrode-topography result.

entries.text: The authors describe classification within 500 ms of articulation onset.
entries.condition: Offline word classification from 0.5-s windows; no online closed-loop latency measurement is reported.

entries.text: The authors claim trial-by-trial classification of up to ten spoken words from surface LFPs at accuracy well above chance.
entries.condition: Single-patient, finite-vocabulary, offline classification; class-specific and word-combination results are reported, not open-vocabulary speech recognition.

entries.text: The authors argue that the best-performing electrode pattern changed by word, supporting independent local neural-processing assemblies.
entries.condition: Interpretation based on word-specific electrode accuracy variation in the single patient; it is not a direct measurement of independent assemblies.
entries.quote: This result suggests that in many cases electrodes recorded activity associated with features not as strongly represented in the data recorded by other nearby micro-electrodes.

entries.text: The authors present micro-ECoG surface potentials as a potential route to intuitive, rapid communication for locked-in patients.
entries.condition: Prospective implication; the experiments classified a finite set of overtly spoken words offline in one patient.

entries.text: The authors distinguish their finite-word classification task from prior work targeting continuous dynamic speech/formant decoding, acknowledging that their dictionary breadth is inherently limited.
entries.condition: Their evaluated output is a closed set of individual word labels rather than continuous speech or formant-frequency synthesis.

entries.text: The study’s one-patient sample limits generalization; the participant had medically refractory epilepsy.
entries.condition: Authors acknowledge epilepsy as relevant to cortical localization and functional interpretation.

entries.text: Epilepsy-related remapping of language areas could affect the anatomical labels and conclusions about FMC versus Wernicke’s activity.
entries.condition: Authors say anatomical labels were supported by available pre- and post-surgical x-rays and photographs, but remapping remained possible.

entries.text: Repeated words over multiple consecutive days may shift processing from cognitive language to memory-based language and affect accuracy.
entries.condition: Same patient repeated a small word set across the four consecutive days; authors say the cognitive-to-memory shift is difficult to confirm or disprove.

entries.text: Pitch and inflection variation in speech may confound classification, and trial selection excluded non-stereotyped pronunciations.
entries.condition: The authors discuss vocal dynamics as potential confounds; the analyzed set was filtered for stereotyped articulation using inflection, pitch, and duration.
entries.quote: vocal dynamics such as pitch or inflection may be the result of dissimilar cortical representation and therefore present a potential confound to the classification process.

entries.text: The reported 500-ms delay may be too slow for conversational speech; actual online feedback and operation were not evaluated.
entries.condition: The paper contrasts discrete word classification with trajectory-based real-time decoding and notes the different feedback requirements.

entries.text: Shorter time windows reduced accuracy; the authors propose HMM/SVM and more advanced feature selection as untested future improvements.
entries.condition: The proposed classifiers and expected improvements were not evaluated in this study; reported analysis used PCA and nearest-centroid classification.

entries.text: The finite dictionary constrains decoded language, and the highest-performing results were for two-word classification.
entries.condition: Ten-word vocabulary was tested, but authors state the highest accuracies occurred in two-word cases.

entries.text: The 4×4 grids covered a small cortical area; broader electrode coverage and optimal spacing remain unresolved.
entries.condition: Authors propose a larger optimized grid as future work; the present arrays had 1-mm spacing.

entries.text: The paper reports a 15-trial train/15-trial decode split from 30 adjacent trials but does not specify split randomization, repeated runs, or cross-validation.
entries.condition: Evaluation-set construction beyond the stated adjacent 15/15 partition is not reported.
entries.quote: For each word, a subset of 30 adjacent trials (15 for training and 15 for decode) containing stereotypical articulation was selected for further analysis.

entries.text: No random seeds, repeated split count, or uncertainty procedure across reruns is reported; reported SDs describe classification results, not repeated training runs.
entries.condition: Applies to all reported classification metrics and comparisons.
entries.quote: Otherwise, for each set of outcomes, the mean, median, and standard deviation were computed for the accuracies of the classification results.

entries.text: No between-speaker test is reported: the same single participant supplies both training and decode trials, so speaker-independent generalization is unknown.
entries.condition: All train/decode conditions are within one male patient; no external participant cohort or speaker-held-out evaluation.

entries.text: The best five electrodes are selected by overall accuracy, but the paper does not identify a separate validation set or show that this selection was independent of decode results.
entries.condition: Relevant to all best-five-channel results for FMC and Wernicke’s area; selection/evaluation data separation is not stated.
entries.quote: Selecting the five electrodes over FMC with best overall accuracy improved average classification accuracy compared with using all 16 electrodes.

entries.text: Normalization is called log-normalization across trials, but its equation and whether parameters use training data only are not given.
entries.condition: Feature normalization could affect train/decode separation; paper does not specify the computation or fit scope.

entries.text: The paper does not report the identity of the sessions/days used for the 30-trial subsets or evaluate generalization across days.
entries.condition: Session duration and four-day schedule are reported, but no per-word session assignment, day-held-out split, or day-wise score is specified.
entries.quote: Sessions lasted approximately one hour and occurred on four consecutive days.

entries.text: Trial selection used inflection, pitch, and duration, but no operational thresholds, rater count, blinding, or agreement measure are stated.

entries.text: The described decoder is nearest-centroid classification over the prompted word set; no language model or other use-time lexical aid is specified.
entries.condition: Closed-set label output from PCA features and trained centroids; no LM-assisted decoding condition is reported.

entries.text: No classifier training/evaluation repository or script is identified; the only linked software is Chronux for spectrogram generation, and no paper-specific repository conditions can be checked.
entries.condition: Chronux is linked as a general signal-analysis package, not as the PCA/nearest-centroid training or evaluation implementation; no repo-path line references are supplied by the paper.

entries.text: Epidural placement and wireless implementation are presented as potential deployment improvements, not tested features.
entries.condition: The study used arrays placed beneath the dura and a wired Neuroport recording system; deployment feasibility is prospective.

entries.text: Task-correlated power varied across sessions; the authors suggest medication, arousal, attention, articulation strength, or electrode micromotion as possible causes.
entries.condition: Observed across sessions in the one participant; causal factors are proposed, not established.
entries.quote: Variability in the task-correlated power was present between sessions

entries.text: Array placement and implantation duration were determined by clinical requirements, limiting control over anatomical placement and recording duration.
entries.condition: The arrays were placed over face motor cortex and Wernicke’s area for the medically required monitoring episode.

entries.text: The authors qualify the FMC-versus-Wernicke comparison: a more cognitive task and different classifier could make Wernicke’s area perform as well as or better than FMC.
entries.condition: The reported comparison applies to overt word repetition and the study’s PCA classification scheme.

entries.text: The authors identify FMC as a promising site for communication prostheses in the studied task.
entries.condition: Inference is limited to one patient, overt word production, finite-vocabulary classification, and the reported task/classifier.

entries.text: The authors report that classification was conducted without patient training before the initial experimental session.
entries.condition: This does not establish absence of practice or learning during the four-day repeated-word experiment.

entries.text: The paper does not report an online closed-loop or real-time user evaluation; operational feedback and deployment performance remain unmeasured.
entries.condition: Methods describe recorded-session analysis and trial decoding, but no online user feedback protocol or deployed system evaluation.

questions.q: How much of the reported accuracy depends on the adjacent-trial split, and were the train/decode partitions repeated or separated by session/day?
questions.answer: The paper reports 15 training and 15 decode trials from 30 adjacent stereotyped trials per word, but gives no split randomization, repeat count, or across-day evaluation protocol.

questions.q: Were the best five electrodes and trial stereotypy criteria selected without using the decode results?
questions.answer: The paper says the five electrodes were selected by best overall accuracy and describes inflection, pitch, and duration judgments, but does not report an independent validation set, thresholds, or selection blinding.

questions.q: Do the results generalize across speakers or sessions, and how was normalization kept independent of decode data?
questions.answer: Only one patient was studied; no speaker-held-out or day-held-out test is reported, and the formula and fit scope for log-normalization are unspecified.

questions.q: Does the reported 500-ms classification support conversational, online communication?
questions.answer: The authors describe a 500-ms delay but concede it may be too slow for conversation; the evaluation was offline and did not test online feedback or control.

questions.q: Was the clinical macro-ECoG grid decoded for comparison, and were neighbour-electrode differences tested against chance variability?
questions.answer: No: only the 32 micro-electrode channels were recorded on the Neuroport (Sec. 2.3); accuracy is compared with uniform chance without a significance test (Sec. 2.6).

questions.q: Evaluation triage: same experiment in Brumberg/Guenther 2009? Guenther partition? Card condition? Chen cohort? Authors' latency caveat?
questions.answer: Same participant, 25 sessions (g9); Guenther offline used two-fold CV within session (g8) and online testing across sessions; Card: first-session sentences from a 50-word vocabulary with a language model (r2, r3); Chen: 43 participants, PCC (ch2, ch3); caveat t90.
